prompt: Match each SPACE dimension to an example measurement.

pairs.right: cycle time and time in queues

prompt: Most of what lessons 1 to 7 measured sits in which two SPACE dimensions?

choices.text: Satisfaction and collaboration
choices.why: Those are exactly the ones the files never touched.

choices.text: Performance and satisfaction
choices.why: Satisfaction needs people's reports; nothing so far asked them.

choices.text: Efficiency and flow, and activity
choices.why: Right. Cycle time and waiting are flow; deployments and items finished are activity.

choices.text: Collaboration and performance
choices.why: Collaboration was untouched, and performance only in the narrow reliability sense.

prompt: Besides its five dimensions, what second axis does the SPACE paper add?

choices.text: Three levels: individual, team, system
choices.why: Right. And the misuse this lesson warns about lives at the first.

choices.text: A score from 0 to 100 for each dimension
choices.why: The framework deliberately offers no score.

choices.text: A ranking of companies by productivity
choices.why: Nothing in it ranks anybody.

choices.text: A list of tools that measure each dimension
choices.why: It is a way of choosing measurements, not a tool list.

prompt: The SPACE paper's first author also led the research behind the DORA metrics: Nicole ___.
Why does the SPACE paper recommend measuring at least three dimensions?

choices.text: Because three numbers fit on one slide
choices.why: Layout is not the reason.

choices.text: Because averaging three dimensions gives a fair score
choices.why: There is no averaging; the dimensions are read side by side.

choices.text: Because fewer than three cannot be computed
choices.why: One can be computed easily; it just hides its costs.

choices.text: So a trade between them becomes visible
choices.why: Right. More activity bought with well-being shows as a falling survey.

prompt: A team's cycle time improved, and its members report in the survey that they cannot focus. What does the lesson make of that?

choices.text: The survey is wrong, because the system data is objective
choices.why: Systems cannot record experience; people are the only source for it.

choices.text: Something has not been measured yet
choices.why: Right. Disagreement between perceptual and system data points at a gap.

choices.text: The cycle time must have been gamed
choices.why: Possible, but the lesson's point is that the two sources see different things.

choices.text: Focus does not matter if cycle time is good
choices.why: That is reading one dimension and ignoring the others.

prompt: The lesson proposes a first set of measures for the Billing team. Which are in it? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Cycle time and its 85th percentile
choices.why: Right. Efficiency and flow.

choices.text: Change failure rate and time to restore
choices.why: Right. Performance, in the reliability sense.

choices.text: A short quarterly survey
choices.why: Right. Satisfaction and well-being.

choices.text: Lines of code per developer
choices.why: That is the individual trap.

prompt: What is a perceptual measure?

choices.text: A measure computed by machine learning
choices.why: It is about who reports it, not how it is computed.

choices.text: A measure that is only estimated
choices.why: It is reported, about one's own experience; not an estimate of a fact.

choices.text: What people report about their own experience
choices.why: Right. The only data about experience, which systems cannot record.

choices.text: A measure shown as a chart
choices.why: Any measure can be drawn.

prompt: What does counting story points per person actually measure?

choices.text: Who estimates high or takes generous items
choices.why: Right. A habit of the individual, rewarded at the team's expense.

choices.text: Each person's real contribution to the team
choices.why: Reviews, unblocking and teaching never become points.

choices.text: How hard each person works
choices.why: Points are estimates, not effort.

choices.text: Which items were the most valuable
choices.why: Points estimate size, and badly; lesson 9.

prompt: Which contributions are invisible to a per-person count of items finished? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Reviewing colleagues' work
choices.why: Right. The rule that cut the Billing team's cycle time lowered each person's count.

choices.text: Unblocking an item stuck on another team
choices.why: Right. The most valuable work of a week can close nothing.

choices.text: Restoring service during the night
choices.why: Right. It leaves an empty commit history the next day.

choices.text: Finishing a large feature alone
choices.why: That one is counted, which is part of the problem.

prompt: If the Billing team were ranked by items finished per person, what would the lesson expect to happen?

choices.text: Throughput would rise, because everybody would try harder
choices.why: Effort would move from reviews to own items, and items would wait in review.

choices.text: Nothing, because the ranking is only information
choices.why: People respond to what is measured, lesson 7.

choices.text: The failure rate would fall
choices.why: Fewer reviews would push it the other way.

choices.text: People would stop reviewing and the queue would return
choices.why: Right. The queue in front of Bia would come back in front of everybody.

prompt: At which level do the DORA and SPACE research measure?

choices.text: The individual developer
choices.why: SPACE warns against ranking individuals; DORA defines its metrics for teams.

choices.text: Teams and systems
choices.why: Right. Using it to measure people is using it for what it was not built to support.

choices.text: Whole countries
choices.why: The surveys span countries, and measure teams.

choices.text: Individual lines of code
choices.why: Neither measures code at that grain.

prompt: Why should a survey use the same few statements every quarter?

choices.text: Because new questions are expensive to write
choices.why: Cost is not the reason.

choices.text: Because people forget the answers otherwise
choices.why: Nobody has to remember an answer.

choices.text: A trend needs the same question
choices.why: Right. Five unchanged statements beat thirty that change.

choices.text: Because anonymity requires it
choices.why: Anonymity is a separate rule.

prompt: In Q3 the six answers to the energy statement were 4, 5, 4, 4, 1 and 4. What is their mean, to one decimal place?
One person answered 1 to the energy statement while the median rose to 4. What should the tech lead do?

choices.text: Make a conversation possible without asking who
choices.why: Right. In a team of six a single low answer is a person, and the survey stays anonymous.

choices.text: Report the median and move on
choices.why: The median hides exactly the answer that matters.

choices.text: Find out who answered 1 from the order of the digits
choices.why: The order means nothing, and trying would end honest answers.

choices.text: Remove the outlier as noise
choices.why: It is a person, not noise.

prompt: Which statement is better worded for a team survey?

choices.text: My colleagues review my work promptly
choices.why: It invites blame of specific people.

choices.text: Rafa is slow to review
choices.why: Naming a person ends the survey's usefulness.

choices.text: The team is productive
choices.why: Too vague to act on, and productivity has five dimensions.

choices.text: When I ask for a review, it arrives quickly
choices.why: Right. A statement about one's own experience of the system.

prompt: In Q2 the answers to the review statement were 1, 1, 2, 2, 1 and 2. What is the median?
Match each legitimate question to the instrument the lesson recommends instead of a ranking.

pairs.left: Does the team have the people it needs?
Does this person deserve a promotion?
pairs.right: evidence of contribution, read in context

prompt: In July the Billing team's work waited in front of one reviewer. What was the answer the lesson describes?

choices.text: Hire a dedicated reviewer
choices.why: No hire was needed.

choices.text: Change who reviews
choices.why: Right. The same people, with reviews done first by everybody.

choices.text: Rate Bia as unproductive
choices.why: The queue was a property of the system, not of Bia.

choices.text: Skip reviews for small items
choices.why: Reviews stayed; who did them changed.

prompt: Why does mixing team measures with individual conversations break both?

choices.text: Because team measures are confidential
choices.why: They are the team's own, and can be shared.

choices.text: Because conversations take too long
choices.why: Time is not the problem.

choices.text: Each side corrupts the other
choices.why: Right. Team measures stop measuring the team; conversations stop being conversations.

choices.text: Because individuals cannot read charts
choices.why: Everybody can; the incentive is the problem.

prompt: A director asks for a monthly list of developers sorted by commits. What is the best response?

choices.text: Ask what he wants to know
choices.why: Right. Behind the ranking is usually a legitimate question with a better answer.

choices.text: Produce it, since the data exists
choices.why: Existing data is not a reason to use it against the team.

choices.text: Produce it but keep it secret from the team
choices.why: A secret ranking is still a ranking, and it will leak.

choices.text: Sort by lines of code instead
choices.why: Same trap, different habit rewarded.

prompt: Put the letters of SPACE in order, by the dimension each stands for.
